activity_context.topic_title: Integrating Functions by Completing the Square

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+8x+17 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 4x+({4}^{2}-{4}^{2})+17 \\  & =({x}^{2}+2\cdot 4x+{4}^{2})-16+17 \\  & =(x+4)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{6}{{x}^{2}+8x+17}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{6}{(x+4)^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\int \frac{1}{1+(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x+4).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=x+4.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $-4$ | $-3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $1$ |

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-3}\frac{6}{{x}^{2}+8x+17}\,\text{d}x & =6{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\operatorname{arctan}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)) \\  & =6(\frac{\pi }{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$
